clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive inherited bone marrow failure syndrome caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in MPL, the receptor for thrombopoietin, resulting in absent or markedly reduced megakaryocytes.

Presents in the neonatal period or early infancy with isolated severe thrombocytopenia and bleeding (petechiae, purpura, mucosal or intracranial haemorrhage) without the limb or radial anomalies seen in thrombocytopenia-absent-radius syndrome.
Unlike thrombocytopenia-absent-radius syndrome, the thumbs are present and there are no characteristic skeletal malformations, an important early distinguishing feature.
Bone marrow shows absent or greatly reduced megakaryocytes with initially preserved erythroid and myeloid lineages.
A defining natural-history feature is progression from isolated thrombocytopenia to trilineage bone marrow failure (aplastic anaemia) during childhood.
There is a recognised predisposition to clonal evolution, including myelodysplastic syndrome and acute leukaemia, warranting long-term haematological surveillance.
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only curative therapy; thrombopoietin-receptor agonists are ineffective because the receptor itself is defective.
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia is an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome caused by biallelic variants in MPL, which encodes the thrombopoietin receptor (c-MPL) expressed on megakaryocytes and haematopoietic stem cells. Thrombopoietin signalling through MPL is essential not only for megakaryocyte proliferation and platelet production but also for the maintenance and self-renewal of the haematopoietic stem cell pool. Complete loss-of-function variants abolish receptor signalling and produce severe, early, persistent thrombocytopenia with virtually absent megakaryocytes, whereas variants retaining partial signalling can give a somewhat milder, more transient early course. Because MPL signalling supports stem cells beyond the megakaryocyte lineage, the initially isolated thrombocytopenia characteristically evolves into progressive pancytopenia and generalised marrow aplasia, and the stressed, genomically vulnerable marrow carries an increased risk of clonal transformation to myelodysplasia and acute leukaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Fanconi anaemia and other inherited bone marrow failure syndromes
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and other inherited thrombocytopenias
MYH9-related disorders and other congenital macrothrombocytopenias
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film confirming isolated thrombocytopenia with normal platelet morphology
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine showing absent/reduced megakaryocytes
Chromosome breakage testing to exclude Fanconi anaemia
Cytogenetics and marrow surveillance for clonal evolution/myelodysplasia
HLA typing of patient and potential related donors for transplantation
redFlags: Neonatal severe thrombocytopenia with mucosal or intracranial haemorrhage
Emerging anaemia or neutropenia signalling progression to marrow failure
Cytogenetic abnormality or dysplasia suggesting clonal evolution
Rising transfusion requirement or transfusion refractoriness
reference.prognosis: Untreated, the disorder carries a poor prognosis owing to bleeding, progression to aplastic anaemia and risk of leukaemic transformation. Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, particularly when performed early from a well-matched donor, can be curative and offers the best long-term outcome.
pitfalls: Assuming thrombopoietin-receptor agonists will help; they are ineffective because the receptor is defective
Confusing the condition with thrombocytopenia-absent-radius syndrome despite the presence of normal thumbs and radii
Regarding it as isolated thrombocytopenia and failing to anticipate and monitor for trilineage marrow failure
Missing the leukaemic predisposition by omitting long-term cytogenetic surveillance
Overlooking Fanconi anaemia without chromosome breakage testing in a child with marrow failure
references: Clinical genetics reference texts on inherited bone marrow failure syndromes
